newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait says OPEC happy with ceiling, prices.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait says OPEC happy with ceiling, prices.

text.p: Kuwait said on Tuesday it was happy with OPEC'S current production ceiling and with prices, but it could demand a higher quota if "circumstances allow".

"I think, and as many members in the Organisation see, it (the production ceiling) fulfilled the desired result," Isa al-Mazeedi said before leaving for Vienna to attend OPEC's ministerial meeting, his first since being appointed Kuwait's Oil Minister in October.
Mazeedi said: "We are all comfortable with the current prices at the time being. In the light of the reports that will be presented (at the meeting) the members will decide.

"At the time being we see the tendency that the current production ceiling goes in line with the requirements of demand, unless the member states see otherwise (then) there will be room to discuss the issue," he added.
When asked if Kuwait -- which has a two million barrel per day (bpd) OPEC quota -- were to demand a higher quota what its target would be, Mazeedi told reporters:

"The production capacity of Kuwait at the time being is 2.5 million bpd. Let us not go ahead of events but our demands would be justice-serving for Kuwait in terms of production capacity and historial status.
"Kuwait's production of oil reached three million bpd at a certain stage," he added.
Asked about Kuwait's previous demand for a 200,000 bpd increase if the total OPEC ceiling was raised, Mazeedi said:
"The present situation is different from that of a year ago or six months ago. We would like to be up to date with the current situation and not with the past one."

OPEC ministers, who meet in Vienna this week, are likely to freeze current output quotas and try to curb violations, in the hope of protecting oil prices against the possible early resumption of sales by Iraq.

Iraq's ambassador at the United Nations, Nizar Hamdoon, said on Monday that Baghdad had agreed to U.N. conditions that had been holding up the implementation of an oil-for-food accord designed to ease the 1991 Gulf War embargo on Iraqi oil exports.
Kuwait's oil minister said: "We heard from some news agencies that Iraq decided to start with the oil-for-food operations. I think we should wait and see the quantity to be exported by Iraq."
Oil prices fell on the Iraq news on Monday, with Jan Brent crude oil futures in London ending 41 cents off at $22.62 per barrel.

While a U.N. Security Council sanctions committee has yet to approve a pricing formula that would actually trigger the resumed flow of Iraqi oil, Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali was optimistic that oil could start in a few weeks.

OPEC had already pencilled in the return of Iraqi oil to its production quota system when it last met in June. The producer group's dilemma is that several of its 11 members are cheating on their assigned quotas, with the consequence that total OPEC volume is already almost one million barrels above its self-assigned ceiling of 25.03 million bpd - and that's even before Iraqi exports flow.
